newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Southeast Asian currencies drop again.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian currencies drop again.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies racked up further losses on Friday as funds continued to pile into the U.S. dollar in a market rife with rumours.
Dealers said liquidity remained very low and spreads wide, exaggerating currency movements.
"Liquidity continues to be a problem so it takes just a few (million) dollars and this market can push it around," said a treasury manager at a U.S. bank in Singapore.

He said there was talk of Asian central banks gearing up for concerted intervention in the face of heavy speculative attacks on regional currencies since the de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso earlier this month.
"There have been all sorts of rumours going through the markets. My own opinion is it could just be people caught short trying to cover back," he added.

The Washington Post newspaper said U.S. Treasury and the International Monetary Fund are on high alert over financial turmoil in emerging markets worldwide, which has sent stocks and currencies plunging.
It quoted officials as saying they were worried the turmoil could slow growth in some of the world's most vibrant economies, which have become key markets for U.S. exports.

The Malaysian ringgit remained weak after sinking to a fresh three-year low of around 2.6080 to the U.S. dollar on selling by offshore funds. It was quoted at 2.6060/90 at 0845 GMT against 2.5970/6000 around noon.
Dealers said the apparent absence of Bank Negara Malaysia from the market, despite talk it had checked rates around the 2.6000 level earlier, contributed to the ringgit's slide.
The ringgit has fallen more than three percent this week, partly due to a perceived change in stance by Malaysian authorities towards allowing market forces to determine the exchange rate.
The Singapore dollar recovered some equilibrium after sinking to a new 30-month low of around 1.4665 against the U.S. dollar.
At 0845 GMT, it was quoted unchanged from its noon levels of 1.4605/15, against an early high of 1.4550/60.
Speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened to stem the currency's slide caused players to turn cautious, dealers said.
"We heard the MAS were up at the 1.4635 level but there's no confirmation," a dealer said. "Ultimately, I don't believe the MAS is too worried about dollar/Sing at these levels."
Dealers said the traditionally robust currency was being affected by declines in regional currencies and a perception the MAS would condone some weakness in it to keep exports competitive.
"They would be uncomfortable if all the neighbours weakened and the Sing dollar did not move," he said.
The Indonesian rupiah fell to a new low of 2,502 to the dollar on spillover weakness.
Indonesian President Suharto was quoted as saying he had asked the country's top finance officials to monitor the situation and take steps against currency speculation.
The Thai baht continued to weaken on commercial dollar demand before a long weekend but its slide was relatively muted, dealers said.
The baht was quoted at 30.350/450 to the dollar onshore at 0830 GMT and 30.300/400 offshore.
The market showed little immediate reaction to news that Japan and Thailand had agreed to cooperate to promote stability in currency markets, using measures including intervention.
